segments.name: The Angus Coast and the Contested Birth

stops.name: Monifieth, the birth three sources cannot agree on
stops.date_confidence: Date attested [A]: Wikipedia's infobox gives 25 November 1874 and nothing consulted disagrees. Place [R], contested three ways and NOT resolved here. English Wikipedia says Monifieth, Angus; Wikidata Q325589 (P19) says Forres, Moray, some 150 km north across the Grampians; German Wikipedia says only Forfarshire; the popular occult reference literature says Broughty Ferry. No parish or statutory register has been consulted. The pin is Monifieth town centre.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of November, in a town on the Angus coast east of Dundee, a son is born and given four names: James Lewis Thomas Chalmers. He will publish under two of them. The place is far less certain than the date. One reference work puts the birth here at Monifieth, another at Forres in Moray two counties north, a third says only Forfarshire, and the occult books say Broughty Ferry. All four repeat the same date without variation. Nobody has read the register.
suggested_refs: The statutory birth register for Angus, November 1874, unconsulted, which would settle Monifieth against Forres against Broughty Ferry

stops.name: Broughty Ferry, the boyhood the popular accounts give him
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout. The Broughty Ferry attribution comes from secondary popularisations, none of them checked against a primary record, and it contradicts English Wikipedia's Monifieth. The 1880 date is invented to order the segment; no source dates his boyhood at all. Coordinates corrected to Broughty Ferry centre (the research pool's 56.465, -2.8778 lay some 550 m out on the west esplanade).
stops.campa: A few miles west along the same shore stands the fishing village turned Dundee suburb where the popular accounts place his childhood. Nothing in the reachable record reconciles this with Monifieth; the two towns are an easy walk apart and the sources simply assert one or the other without argument. Either way the boy grows up looking at the same water, and the coast here is one long argument with it: the Tay running wide into the North Sea, the esplanade, the sandbanks out in the estuary that take ships down.
suggested_refs: The Broughty Ferry tradition of Spence's boyhood, unreconciled with the Monifieth birth claim

stops.campa: He marries Helen Bruce. The year is attested and nothing else is: no source consulted names the church, the street, the witnesses, or her people. She will be his wife for forty-three years, live through every book he writes but the last handful, and be laid in his grave thirteen years before he joins her in it. The marriage gets one line in a reference article; the man gets forty volumes. Of Helen Bruce herself the reachable record holds two numbers, 1899 and 1942, and no third fact.

stops.name: Cockburn Street, joining The Scotsman
stops.date_confidence: [A] that Spence was at The Scotsman from 1899 to 1906 (Wikipedia). The Cockburn Street office is attested for the paper rather than separately for his desk (Wikipedia, 'The Scotsman', for the Peddie & Kinnear building). Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He joins The Scotsman in the year he marries, in the offices on Cockburn Street, the curving Victorian stair of a street that Peddie and Kinnear cut down from the High Street toward Waverley. He is twenty-four. Nothing in the work forecasts the Popol Vuh or a drowned continent, and the habit it builds is the one that carries him for the next half century: a length and a deadline, every day of the week. For seven years it is the work of any Edinburgh sub-editor, copy in and proofs out, the wire, the night desk, a column measure to fill before the presses run.

stops.campa: For one year he edits The Edinburgh Magazine, a second post held alongside or just after the newspaper. The sources give the span and nothing else, not an address and not a line about the contents. It is the first thing he directs rather than serves. He is thirty. Whatever he learns that year about commissioning, cutting and filling a whole publication he will spend the next four decades applying to books instead. He will occupy the new offices for barely a year before the editorship ends.

stops.campa: His run at The Scotsman closes after seven years. The sources give no reason and no incident: an editorship begins in 1899 and ends in 1906, and the next entry is London. He is thirty-one, married, and has published nothing at all. Everything that will carry his name lies on the far side of this date: the mythologies, the encyclopaedias, the five books on Atlantis, the Scots verse, the nationalist argument. His whole working life so far has gone into setting other men's pages to other men's schedules. Why he left is not recorded.

stops.campa: He goes south to edit The British Weekly, the nonconformist religious paper William Robertson Nicoll founded and Hodder and Stoughton publish out of Paternoster Row, the street of the London book trade. It is the only sustained period of his life documented anywhere outside Scotland, and it runs three years. He is thirty-two, editing sermons and church affairs by day and reading his way into Mesoamerica on his own hours. The exact office is not attested; the publisher's house on Paternoster Row stands in for it here.

stops.date_confidence: Publication [A] (Wikipedia). Place of composition [R]: London is inferred from his known posting in 1908 and is not independently attested. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: In the middle of the London posting he publishes The Popol Vuh, an English popularisation of the Quiche Maya book of creation: the gods deliberating over the dark water, the men of mud who dissolve in it, the men of wood who are destroyed, the twins who go down into Xibalba to play ball with the lords of death. He is a newspaper editor with no field training and no Mayan, working from the printed translations of other men. It is his first book. He is thirty-four.

From this year until his death forty-six years later he holds no salaried post, edits no paper, and lives by writing books: mythology, folklore, occultism, verse, nationalist argument, roughly a volume a year and often more than one. Edinburgh takes him back as a private author with a study and a subject. He is thirty-four, and the arrangement he settles into now, no employer and no faculty, holds without a break for the rest of his life. segments.name: The Shelf of Peoples: One Mythology a Year

stops.name: Edinburgh, A Dictionary of Mythology
stops.date_confidence: Publication year [A] (Wikipedia). Place of composition [R], inferred from his Edinburgh residence. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: A Dictionary of Mythology appears, the first of the reference works, and the form turns out to suit him exactly. The alphabet imposes the order; the entry imposes the brevity; a man who has spent seven years writing to a column measure can fill a thousand of them without strain. He is doing no fieldwork and does not pretend to. What the reading public of 1910 wants is the gods of the world gathered into one volume, in English, at a price it can pay. He supplies it.
suggested_refs: A Dictionary of Mythology (1910), the first of Spence's alphabetical reference works

stops.date_confidence: Publication year [A] (Wikipedia). stops.campa: The Myths of Mexico and Peru appears from Harrap, and its first chapter opens by closing a door: the civilisations of the New World are indigenous, and require no Egyptians, no Phoenicians, no seeding from outside. The same author will spend the following decade arguing that a drowned Atlantic continent seeded them. He does not present this as a reversal, and no source consulted records him reconciling the two statements. The book itself is a straight retelling of Aztec, Maya and Inca myth, and it stays in print for decades.
stops.quote: There is now no question as to the indigenous origin of the civilisations of Mexico, Central America, and Peru.
stops.quote_source: Lewis Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru (Harrap, 1913), chapter I, opening sentence

stops.name: Edinburgh, the romance of old America
stops.date_confidence: Same book, same year; the June date is invented purely to order this stop after the previous one within the segment. Quotation verified [A] from the Internet Archive full text of the 1913 Preface, identifier mythsofmexicoper01spen. stops.campa: The Preface to the same volume says out loud what the whole shelf is for. He is not writing for Assyriologists or Americanists. He is writing for a reader who has been told that the Americas have no history worth the name and has never been shown the sources that would prove otherwise. What remains, he says on the same page, is the romance of old America, its golden empires, its sole exemplars of civilisation. The argument is not that the general reader is stupid. It is that the material has been locked in monographs and Spanish chronicles.
stops.quote: It is only because the sources of that history are unknown to the general reader that such assurance upon the lack of it exists.
stops.quote_source: Lewis Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru (1913), Preface; archive.org identifier mythsofmexicoper01spen

stops.name: Edinburgh, The Myths of the North American Indians
stops.date_confidence: Publication year [A] (Wikipedia). Place of composition [R]. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: The North American volume follows within a year: the same shape applied to another continent, with origin stories, culture heroes, the trickster, the ceremonies, arranged for a reader who will never see a reservation. It is published as Europe goes to war. Spence is forty and keeps working. Between 1908 and 1921 he produces a book on the myths of a different people almost every year, a whole world mythology for the general reader, all of it written at one desk in Edinburgh.

stops.name: Edinburgh, Myths and Legends of Babylonia and Assyria
stops.date_confidence: Publication year [A] (Wikipedia; Wikisource author page). Note that the Wikisource author page mirrors Wikipedia's bibliography and is not an independent witness. Place of composition [R]. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Myths and Legends of Babylonia and Assyria is published in London in the middle of the war. The subject is Gilgamesh, the descent of Ishtar, Marduk against Tiamat, the flood tablet: a literature dug out of Nineveh within living memory and still being argued over by the men who can read it. Spence is not one of them. He works from their translations for readers who will never see a cuneiform sign, and he does it while the British army is fighting across the country the tablets came from.

The research pool called it 'An Encyclopaedia of Occultism and Parapsychology', which is a conflation with a later and different work, Leslie Shepard's expanded multi-volume edition built on Spence and Nandor Fodor, indexed separately by Open Library. stops.campa: An Encyclopaedia of Occultism appears from George Routledge and Sons: alphabetical, comprehensive, and the most durable thing he ever makes. Mediums, grimoires, secret orders, hauntings, alchemists, saints and outright frauds, each given an entry and a length proportioned to the evidence rather than to the compiler's belief. English publishers now apply to him when they want the occult surveyed by somebody who will neither sneer at it nor swear to it. He takes the commission the way a journalist takes an assignment. He is forty-five, working alone.
suggested_refs: An Encyclopaedia of Occultism (George Routledge & Sons, 1920), not to be confused with the later Shepard expansion under a similar title

stops.name: Edinburgh, An Introduction to Mythology
stops.date_confidence: Publication year [A] (Wikipedia). Place of composition [R]. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: An Introduction to Mythology, the general statement standing behind twelve years of particular volumes. Having retold the myths of Mexico, Peru, North America, Babylonia and Assyria one people at a time, he now sets out what he takes myth to be and how he thinks it should be read. He is arguing inside a discipline that will not have him: no chair, no excavation, no fieldwork, no doctorate. What he has is the whole shelf, read, and a readership no professional Assyriologist will reach in a lifetime. Whether any professional in that discipline answered the book is not recorded in anything consulted.

stops.campa: The Gods of Mexico: not a retelling for the general reader but a systematic treatment of the Mexican pantheon, deity by deity, attribute by attribute, worked out of the codices and the Spanish chroniclers. It is the book of a man who has read the same sources for fifteen years and now wants to argue with the specialists instead of translating for the public. The specialists largely do not answer. In the same year he publishes a book of Scots verse, and the two readerships never meet.

stops.name: Edinburgh, The Problem of Atlantis
stops.date_confidence: Publication year [A] (Wikipedia), which also explicitly names the Donnelly lineage. The reviewer 'R.N.R.B.' and the review's wording are [R]: the citation is The Geographical Journal 64:2 (August 1924), pp. 181-182, but the JSTOR scan of the printed page is paywalled and was NOT inspected; the quotation reaches this file only through Wikipedia. stops.campa: The Problem of Atlantis, and the turn that will define him for a century. Ignatius Donnelly had revived Plato's island for the nineteenth century, mustering geology, botany and comparative myth to argue that a mid-Atlantic continent sank and seeded the civilisations on both its shores. Spence takes the case up for the twentieth, with wider reading and the same conclusion. The Geographical Journal reviews him that August, grants that he is industrious, and does not believe a word of it. He will publish four more books on the subject.
stops.quote: Mr. Spence is an industrious writer, and, even if he fails to convince, has done service in marshalling the evidence and has produced an entertaining volume which is well worth reading.
stops.quote_source: R.N.R.B., review of The Problem of Atlantis, The Geographical Journal 64:2 (August 1924), pp. 181-182, as quoted on Wikipedia; the printed page has not been inspected
suggested_refs: Ignatius Donnelly, Atlantis: The Antediluvian World (1882), the book Spence takes up

It grants him industry, evidence marshalled, an entertaining volume well worth reading, and then puts in one clause the thing that will be said about him for the next hundred years. stops.date_confidence: Same book, same year; the April date is invented purely to order this stop after the previous one. stops.campa: Plato, he insists, was not writing allegory. The Timaeus and the Critias set down what Solon brought back from the priests of Egypt, and they meant it as record. Every one of the five Atlantis books rests on that single reading: if the account is testimony, then the geology, the myth-parallels and the drowned coastlines stop being decoration and become corroboration. He states it flatly, in his own early pages, before any evidence is produced, and lets the rest answer to it.

stops.name: Edinburgh, the testimony brought back by Solon
stops.date_confidence: Same book; the June date is invented purely to order this stop between the two on either side. The quotation is Plato's Timaeus in the translation Spence reproduces inside his own pages, verified [A] from the archive.org scan of The History of Atlantis. NO stop is placed at Sais or anywhere in Egypt: Spence never travelled there, the temple-of-Neith scene belongs to Plato's own file at the canonical pin 30.9647, 30.7683, and it is cited here as a source rather than staged as a scene.
stops.campa: The transmission he stakes everything on is a chain of hearsay that he treats as a chain of custody. Egyptian priests at Sais tell Solon what their records hold; Solon carries it to Athens; the account descends through Critias to Plato, and Plato sets it down. Spence reproduces the Egyptian sentences in his own pages: the exceeding great earthquakes and floods, the one day and night of destruction, the warriors swallowed by the ground and the island going down after them. He never goes to Egypt and never needs to. The text is the evidence, and he reads it as a deposition.
stops.quote: But in later time, after there had been exceeding great earthquakes and floods, there fell one day and night of destruction; and the warriors in your land all in one body were swallowed up by the earth, and in like manner did the island Atlantis sink beneath the sea and vanish away.
stops.quote_source: Plato, Timaeus, in the translation reproduced by Lewis Spence in The History of Atlantis (1926); archive.org identifier historyofatlanti00spenuoft
suggested_refs: Plato, Timaeus and Critias, the Solon transmission, which belongs as a scene to Plato's own file and not to Spence's

stops.date_confidence: Same book; the August date is invented purely to order this stop within the segment. Quotation verified [A] from the archive.org scan. stops.campa: Inside the Atlantis books runs a thread that is not Mexican at all. Lyonesse, the drowned country west of Cornwall that Arthurian romance will not stop remembering; Albion and Iberius, gods he groups with Atlas; the British islands read as the surviving eastern rim of the lost land. He calls British tradition the touchstone of Atlantean history. These are the same years he is giving to Scots verse and to a nationalist party, and nothing in the record shows him treating the recovery of a drowned continent and the recovery of a lapsed country as two different jobs.
stops.quote: British tradition, indeed, is the touchstone of Atlantean history, and the identification of Lyonesse with Atlantis, and the grouping of Atlas with the British gods, Albion and Iberius, should go far to prove the ancient association of our islands with the sunken continent.
